body.p: By this response, claims 1, 4-12, 14-17, and 20-22 are pending. Claims 1, 7, 8, 11, and 17 are amended. Claims 3, 13, and 19 are canceled. No new subject matter is added.
I. Rejections Under 35 U.S.C. 4 102 and 103

In the final Office action, claims 1-3, 5, 11-14, and 17-19 are rejected are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Vallart et al. US 20160327958 ("Vallart"). Claims 4, 15, and 20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Vallart in view of Romana et al. US 20170008619 ("Romana"). Claims 6-8 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Vallart in view of White EP 3208190 ("White"). Claims 9-10 and 16 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Vallart in view of Waltner et al. US 20180305038 ("Waltner").
In the Advisory Action, the Examiner also noted an additional reference (US 2017/0008619 - Romana) deemed to be relevant to the claims.
a. Independent Claim 1

Amended independent claim 1 recites a control system for an aircraft including, among other things, a controller configured to receive the pilot input via the pilot input device, receive a sensed force on the landing gear via the first sensor, calculate an output command based at least on the pilot input and the force on the landing gear, wherein the controller calculates the output command by calculating a correction factor, wherein the pilot input and the sensed force on the landing gear are inputs used to calculate the correction factor, and transmit the output command to control the aircraft, wherein the controller determines the correction factor using a PID control mode when the aircraft is in a landed state.

The Examiner rejects independent claim 1 as being anticipated by Vallart. The Examiner also notes that Romana is relevant to claim 1. Claim 1 is amended to provide further clarity on calculating the correction factor using the pilot input and the sensed force on the landing gear as inputs. Additionally, claim 1 is amended to specify that the controller determines the correction factor using a PID control mode when the aircraft is in a landed state. Both Vallart and Romana fail to teach or suggest determining a correction factor using a PID control mode when the
aircraft is in a landed state. Vallart teaches away from using a PID control during the landed state. Romana does not discuss the use of PID controls.
As brief summary, Vallart explains that the control laws generally make use of an

adjuster defined by either a proportional gain or an integral time constant, but that there are many dangers and problems associated with using these types of adjusters if used during the landed state. See Vallart [0015]-[0035. Accordingly, the proportional gain and integral time constant are typically reduced or canceled at the first sign of the rotorcraft making contact with the ground. Vallart [0023]-[0026]. Vallart's goal is to identify a solution for using these types of adjusters during an intermediate state called the "touching state" in which one the rotorcraft is between the in-flight state and the fully landed state. However, once the rotorcraft is in a fully landed state, Vallart no longer uses an adjuster with either proportional gain or an integral time constant. This is because the initial dangers and concerns expressed by Vallart still remain. Therefore, Vallart teaches away from the use of a PID control mode (which uses proportional gains and an integral time constant) during the landed state.

In order to fully appreciate why Vallart teaches away from using a PID control during the landed state, it is important to understand the problem and solution addressed by Vallart. In the background section, Vallart explains that the topography of the landing sites may be extremely varied. Vallart [0009]. Flight crews may face complex phase of landing, particularly between flight and the fully landed state of the rotorcraft. Vallart [0014]. This is typical when personnel, such as physicians or rescue workers, are disembarked on sloping terrain. Vallart [0014]. Landings on sloping terrain are some of the most delicate maneuvers that rotorcraft crews are required to perform. Vallart [0014]. In these situations, the flight crew performs a maneuver on the slopped terrain by positioning the nose of the rotorcraft facing the rising terrain, with the forward landing gear in contact with the ground and with the rear landing gear off the ground. Vallart [0014].

The problem Vallart seeks to address is that the control law used to operate the rotorcraft is dramatically different depending on whether the rotorcraft is in flight or in contact with the ground. This can be problematic when doing complex maneuvers like the one described above, in which the rotorcraft is essentially in a transition state between flight and fully landed state,
with one landing gear is on the ground and the other two are off the ground. Therefore, Vallart seeks to identify a solution for operating the rotorcraft when it is in a "touching" state.
Vallart explains that there are significantly different goals and risk associated with using the appropriate control logic during each of the flight states:

In point of fact, the control of a rotorcraft differs depending on whether the rotorcraft is in flight or in contact with the ground. Accordingly, different control laws are traditionally used to control a rotor, depending on whether the rotorcraft is or is not in contact with the ground. If the in-flight control law is retained when the rotorcraft is in contact with the ground, the preservation of the control goal would be negatively affected by this contact with the ground. The use of such a control law when the rotorcraft is in contact with the ground could, for example, cause the tilting of the rotor or even an
amplification of ground resonance. Vallart [001S]

Therefore, it is customary to use a ground control law that is very different from the in-flight control law. Thus, the structure and the benefits of the ground law usually differ greatly from those of the in-flight control law. The in-flight control law favors the maintenance of flight parameters, whereas the goal of the ground control law consists of directly controlling the position of the rotor. Therefore, control of the helicopter must be adapted between these two operating modes, while maintaining a maximum level of assistance and the controllability of the aircraft during the transition phase between on-the-ground and in-flight situations. This adaptation of the control modes assumes the availability of information about the status of the aircraft in relation to the ground. This information is usually referred to collectively as the "ground/flight logic".
Vallart [0016]

Vallart explains that the control laws generally make use of an adjuster defined by either a proportional gain or an integral time constant. Vallart [0017]. The integral time constant makes it possible to ensure the long-term stability of a parameter, such as attitude or the traveling speed of the rotorcraft. Vallart [0017]. Meanwhile, the proportional gain contributes towards the short-term stability of the parameter. Vallart [0018]. However, Vallart warns that when these types of adjusters are activated on the ground, the proportional gains and the integral time constant can have dangerous effects, such as tilting the helicopter on the ground (i.e., "roll over"). Vallart [0019]. Therefore, Vallart explains that "it is known that in order to avoid these risks, simpler control law can be implemented, and the proportional gains of the control laws can be reduced when contact with the ground is detected." Vallart [0023]. Simplification

of the control law can also be accomplished "by canceling the integral adjustment at the first sign of contact with the ground." Vallart [0025]. Alternatively, the integral adjustment may be retained via an active adjuster during the landing phase, but the integrator performs an integration until the static error becomes null. Vallart [0029].

Vallart sets out to establish a control system in which the integrating adjuster can remain active while the rotorcraft is in the "touching" state so that the pilot can retain full control authority during this flight state. Vallart [0057] (see also, Vallart [0056]-[0060]). However, once the rotorcraft is in the landed state, the integrated adjuster is not in use. Vallart [0065]. Vallart uses sensors to identify which state the rotorcraft is in as well as which control law should be utilized, as follows:
" The "in flight" state is identified when each of the reaction forces F1, F2, and F3
are simultaneously lower than the low threshold (Ss) value. Vallart [0044]. In
this flight state, the first control law is used. Vallart [0046].
" The "touching" state is identified when the following two conditions are met: 1)
the reaction force F 1 is greater than the low threshold (Ss) value but lower than
the high threshold (SH); and 2) each of the reaction forces F2 and F3 are lower
than the low threshold (Ss) value. Vallart [0041]-[0043]. In this flight state, the
first control law is used. Vallart [0047].
" The "landed" state is identified when the force on the landing gear is greater than
the high threshold (SH). Vallart [0065J. In this state, a third/different control law
is used which does not use an integrated adjuster. Vallart [0065].

Significantly, when the landed state of the rotorcraft is identified, "a new control law is implemented with a different structure than the first and second control laws. In particular, such a new law may be a direct or proportional law, and may not included an integrated adjuster." Vallart [0065J. Therefore, Vallart does not use a PID control (i.e., with an integrated adjuster) when in the landed state. This is likely due to the number of dangers and concerns described by Vallart throughout the specification. Accordingly, Vallart teaches away from using a PID control mode during a landed state.
Romana fails to cure the deficiencies of Vallart. Romana does not discuss the use of

adjusters such as a direct, proportional, or integral adjusters. Rather Romana merely discusses the use of differential breaking to correct the direction of travel of the aircraft. Therefore, neither Vallart nor Romana, together or alone, teaches or suggests determining a correction factor using a PID control mode when the aircraft is in a landed state, as recited in claim 1. Therefore, Applicant respectfully contends that claim 1 is allowable for at least these reasons, in addition to other reasons not explicitly discussed herein. Claims 4-10 ultimately depend from claim 1, and therefore, are allowable for at least the same reasons, in addition to independent reasons not explicitly discussed herein.
b. Independent Claim 11

Amended independent claim 11 recites a method of controlling an aircraft including, among other things, receiving a pilot input including a setpoint, receiving a first signal from a first sensor positioned on a landing gear of the aircraft, and calculating a first correction factor, wherein the setpoint and the first signal are inputs used to calculate the first correction factor, wherein, when the aircraft is in a landed state, the controller is configured to determine the correction factor using a PID control mode.

The Examiner rejects independent claim 11 as being anticipated by Vallart and notes the relevancy of Romana to claim 11. As explained in further detail above with respect to claim 1, Vallart fails to teach or suggest that when the aircraft is in a landed state, the controller is configured to determine the correction factor using a PID control mode. Rather, Vallart teaches against the use of a PID control during a landed state due to the dangers and complications of using such a control mode in the landed state. While Vallart discusses the use of integrating adjusters during the flight state and the touching state, Vallart explains that once the landed state is identified, a new control law is implemented in which direct and proportional control law is used and the integrating adjuster is not included. Therefore, Vallart fail to disclose the use of an integrated adjuster during a landed state. In fact, Vallart teaches away from using an integrated adjuster during the landed state due to the dangers and problems associated with using such a control law during the landed state. Therefore, Vallart does not disclose each and every element of claim 11.
Romana fails to cure the deficiencies of Vallart. Romana does not discuss the use of

adjusters such as a direct, proportional, or integral adjusters. Rather Romana merely discusses the use of differential breaking to correct the direction of travel of the aircraft. Therefore, neither Vallart nor Romana, together or alone, teaches or suggests that when the aircraft is in a landed state, the controller is configured to determine the correction factor using a PID control mode, as recited in claim 11. Therefore, Applicant respectfully contends that claim 11 is allowable for at least these reasons, in addition to other reasons not explicitly discussed herein. Claims 12 and 14-16 ultimately depend from claim 11, and therefore, are allowable for at least the same reasons, in addition to independent reasons not explicitly discussed herein.

II. Conclusion

In view of the amendments and remarks presented herein, it is respectfully submitted that the claims are in condition for allowance. Therefore, Applicant requests withdrawal of the present rejections and/or objections in order to allow the application to be allowed.
